doc.title: Al Vollmer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 8, 2017

chapter: Founding the Harlem Blues and Jazz Band
title: Connecticut Traditional Jazz Club and relining Albert Burbank's denture
summary: He joined Bill Bissonnette's club, hosted visiting New Orleans musicians at home, and fixed singer Albert Burbank's denture.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: But I mean also because of the dentistry I was able to help many of the musicians. I’ve had incredible patients. I mean I’ll just give one little story. How I started, before I got involved and had the big house, I belonged to the Connecticut Traditional Jazz Club, which was formed by Bill Bissonnette, who was a trombonist and a absolute rabid New Orleans — nothing is any good if it’s not from New Orleans. Anyway, he had his own band and he couldn’t run a club and put on the concerts and all that, so he put out a call for people to come and help him run a club. And what happened, the way I saw it, was you probably — I don’t know if you know — there was Indian Joe a loft on Sixth Avenue upstairs, had a record shop. Okay. He was apparently an Indian and he had all these jazz records. It was just jazz records on the second floor. And I used to go there. And on the door, entering into the record shop was a poster saying that Bill Bissonnette had put out, asking for people to come and help him. So I answered that. And some of our meetings were up in Hamden, Connecticut, I mean I drove two hours to a meeting and would come home late and all of that. But anyway we were non-profit. We put on concerts in various Holiday Inns. Eight concerts a year. This was before Jaffe had organized it in New Orleans, we could call up the guys directly, we brought them up on the red eye, that was the cheapest, we put them up in our homes. And at that time I didn’t have the big house, and I would put them up upstairs in my house and they all wanted to come to me because I could reline their dentures and so on and so forth. They knew I had my dental office in my house at that time. So I remember Albert Burbank and he said, “What is your name?” And I said, “My name is Al for Albert.” “Oh, that’s an easy name for me to remember,” he said.
